x: A − B keeps the elements of A that are not in B: removing 2 and 4 leaves {1, 3, 5}. {6} is B − A, {2, 4} is A ∩ B and {1, 3, 5, 6} is the symmetric difference.

q: A and B are subsets of a universal set U, and ′ denotes the complement. Which set equals (A ∪ B)′?
x: By De Morgan's law the complement of a union is the intersection of the complements: (A ∪ B)′ = A′ ∩ B′. A′ ∪ B′ is the complement of A ∩ B instead.

q: A = {1, 2, 3, 4} and B = {3, 4, 5}. What is the symmetric difference (A − B) ∪ (B − A)?
x: A − B = {1, 2} and B − A = {5}, so their union is {1, 2, 5}. Check: it is A ∪ B = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5} with A ∩ B = {3, 4} removed.

q: P(S) denotes the power set of a set S and ∅ is the empty set. How many elements does P(P(∅)) have?
x: P(∅) = {∅} has 1 element, so its power set has 2¹ = 2 elements: ∅ and {∅}. Thinking P(∅) is empty gives P(P(∅)) = {∅}, with only 1 element.

q: Of 100 students, 50 like tea, 40 like coffee and 30 like juice; 15 like tea and coffee, 10 like coffee and juice, 12 like tea and juice, and 5 like all three. How many like none of the three?
x: n(T ∪ C ∪ J) = 50 + 40 + 30 − 15 − 10 − 12 + 5 = 88, so 100 − 88 = 12 like none. Forgetting to add back the 5 who like all three gives 17.

q: Sets A and B satisfy A ∪ B = A ∩ B. What must be true?
o: A is a proper subset of B
x: A ⊆ A ∪ B = A ∩ B ⊆ B, so A ⊆ B, and in the same way B ⊆ A. Hence A = B. Check with A = B = {1}: both sides are {1}; with B = ∅ and A = {1} the sides are {1} and ∅.

q: A = {1, 2} and B = {2, 3}. What is (A × B) ∩ (B × A)?
x: A × B = {(1, 2), (1, 3), (2, 2), (2, 3)} and B × A = {(2, 1), (2, 2), (3, 1), (3, 2)}. Only (2, 2) is in both. Order matters in a pair, so (2, 3) and (3, 2) are different elements.

q: What is the converse of the statement “If a number is divisible by 4, then it is even”?
o: If a number is not even, then it is not divisible by 4.
If a number is even, then it is divisible by 4.
If a number is not divisible by 4, then it is not even.
A number is divisible by 4 and it is not even.
x: The converse of p → q is q → p: “If a number is even, then it is divisible by 4” (false, e.g. 6). ~q → ~p is the contrapositive and ~p → ~q is the inverse.

q: In the 8-row truth table for the statements p, q and r, in how many rows is (p → q) ∧ (q → r) true?
x: Both implications hold exactly when no true letter is followed by a false one in the order p, q, r: FFF, FFT, FTT and TTT. That is 4 rows; for example TFT fails because p → q is false there.

q: Which of these statements is a contradiction, that is, false for every choice of truth values of p and q?
x: p ∧ ~q is true exactly when p → q is false, so (p → q) ∧ (p ∧ ~q) is always false. Joining the same two parts with ∨ gives a tautology; ~p ∧ (p ∨ q) is true when p is false and q true, and p ∧ (q → p) is true when p is true.

q: The function f: Z → Z is defined by f(x) = 2x + 1. Which statement is true?
o: f is one-one but not onto
f is onto but not one-one
f is both one-one and onto
f is neither one-one nor onto
x: 2a + 1 = 2b + 1 gives a = b, so f is one-one. But f(x) is always odd, so an even integer such as 2 is never an image: f is not onto Z. (As a function on R the same rule would be a bijection.)

q: f(x) = (x − 1)/(x + 2) for x ≠ −2. What is f⁻¹(2)?
x: f⁻¹(2) is the x with f(x) = 2: x − 1 = 2(x + 2), so x = −5. Check: f(−5) = −6/−3 = 2. Computing f(2) = 1/4 instead is the usual slip.

q: Which of these relations on R is a function whose inverse relation is also a function?
x: y = x³ is one-one and onto R, so its inverse y = ∛x is again a function. y = x² and y = |x| are not one-one (x = 2 and x = −2 give the same y), and y² = x is not a function at all (x = 4 gives y = ±2).

q: In the group {0, 1, 2, 3} under addition modulo 4, what is the inverse of 3?
x: The identity is 0, and 3 + 1 = 4 ≡ 0 (mod 4), so the inverse of 3 is 1. Check: 3 + 3 = 6 ≡ 2 and 3 + 0 = 3, neither is the identity.

q: a and b are elements of a group. Which expression is always equal to (ab)⁻¹?
x: (ab)(b⁻¹a⁻¹) = a(bb⁻¹)a⁻¹ = aa⁻¹ = e, so (ab)⁻¹ = b⁻¹a⁻¹: the order reverses. a⁻¹b⁻¹ is equal to it only in a commutative group.

q: Which of these binary operations on R is commutative but NOT associative?
x: (a + b)/2 = (b + a)/2, but (0 * 0) * 4 = 0 * 4 = 2 while 0 * (0 * 4) = 0 * 2 = 1. a + b + 1 is commutative and associative, a * b = a is associative but not commutative, and a − b is neither.
